steps.title: See it
steps.text: The pawn moves straight forward, one square at a time, and never backward. It captures in a different way: one square diagonally forward. So this pawn can step to d5, or capture the knight on e5.

steps.title: Try it
steps.text: Capture the knight on e4, then walk the pawn on to e6.

pages.text: A pawn that has not moved yet, on its starting rank, may step two squares forward instead of one. This is called a double step. Many games start with a pawn's double step to the middle of the board.

The pawn is worth the least of all the pieces, so it makes a fine attacker. When a pawn attacks a bigger piece, that piece must run. Here the pawn steps to d5 and attacks both knights at once. Black can save only one of them.
A pawn that reaches the far side of the board becomes a stronger piece, almost always a queen. This is called promotion, and it has its own lesson later. Here the pawn on d7 is one step away.

puzzles.hint: A pawn captures one square diagonally forward. It can reach two pieces here: pick the rook.

puzzles.prompt: Win the black bishop in two moves. A bishop moves diagonally, as far as it likes, and can't jump over pieces.
puzzles.hint: The bishop has only one open diagonal. Block it with a pawn that another pawn protects.
A pawn gives check too. Your king guards the squares around the black king.

puzzles.prompt: Checkmate in two moves, with your pawns. Your knight on d7 guards f8, so the black king can't go there.
puzzles.hint: Start with a pawn capture that gives check. The black king will have only one square left.
